Basic Electricity.intro: Electric current is the flow of charge. Understanding the basic concepts of voltage, current and resistance is essential for all of P2.
Basic Electricity.mnemonic: "Very Intelligent Rabbits" — V = IR (Voltage = Current × Resistance) — Ohm's Law in one phrase.

🖼️
Diagram: Basic Electricity — V, I, R
Image coming soon

sections.title: Current, Voltage and Resistance
sections.text: These three quantities describe the electrical behaviour of any circuit component and are linked by Ohm's Law.
points: Current (I) — rate of flow of charge; measured in amperes (A); 1 A = 1 coulomb per second
Voltage/potential difference (V) — energy transferred per unit charge; measured in volts (V)
Resistance (R) — opposition to current flow; measured in ohms (Ω); caused by collisions of electrons with the lattice
Relationship — increasing voltage increases current; increasing resistance decreases current
Units summary — Amps (A), Volts (V), Ohms (Ω), Coulombs (C) — know these for every question

sections.title: Ohm's Law
sections.text: Ohm's Law relates voltage, current, and resistance for ohmic conductors and is the most important equation in electricity.
points: V = IR — rearranged: I = V/R (find current) and R = V/I (find resistance)
Example — a 12 V battery drives a current through a 4 Ω resistor: I = 12/4 = 3 A
Ohmic conductor — resistance stays constant at constant temperature (e.g. resistor, metal wire)
Filament bulb — non-ohmic; as it heats up, resistance increases (I-V graph curves)
Diode — non-ohmic; only conducts in one direction; very high resistance in reverse direction

callout.label: Formula
callout.text: V = I × R (Voltage = Current × Resistance). Rearranged: I = V/R and R = V/I. An ohmic conductor has constant resistance.

sections.title: Charge Flow
sections.text: Charge is the fundamental quantity in electricity — current measures the rate at which charge flows.
points: Q = It — charge Q in coulombs (C), current I in amperes (A), time t in seconds (s)
Example — a current of 2 A flows for 30 s: Q = 2 × 30 = 60 C
Electron flow — in metals, current is carried by free electrons moving through the lattice
Conventional current — defined as flowing from positive to negative terminal (opposite to electron flow)
One coulomb — the charge transferred when 1 A flows for 1 second

callout.label: Formula
callout.text: Q = I × t (Charge = Current × Time). Charge is measured in coulombs (C).

keyTerms.def: The rate of flow of electric charge — measured in amperes (A)
The energy transferred per unit charge — measured in volts (V)
Opposition to current flow — measured in ohms (Ω)
V = IR — voltage, current and resistance are proportionally related in ohmic conductors
A component whose resistance remains constant as voltage changes, at constant temperature
The unit of electric charge (C) — the charge transferred by 1 A flowing for 1 second
A component whose resistance changes with current or voltage, e.g. filament bulb, diode

examTips: V = IR is the most used formula in electricity — learn the triangle: cover the quantity you want to find.
Ohmic conductors have constant resistance. Filament bulbs and diodes do not — their I-V graphs are not straight lines.
Charge = current × time. Charge is in coulombs (C) — don't confuse C (coulombs) with °C (temperature).
commonMistakes: Confusing current (flow of charge) with voltage (energy per charge) — they are very different quantities.
Saying current is 'used up' in a circuit — current is the same everywhere in a series circuit.
Forgetting to check units in charge calculations — time must be in seconds, not minutes.
clozePassages: Electric current is the flow of charge through a circuit, measured in amperes (A). Potential difference (voltage) is the energy transferred per unit charge, measured in volts (V). Resistance is the opposition to current flow, measured in ohms (Ω). These three quantities are related by Ohm's Law: V = IR. Increasing resistance reduces current for a given potential difference.

Ohm's Law states that the current through a conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference across it, provided temperature remains constant. A component that obeys Ohm's Law is called an ohmic conductor. The relationship V = IR can be rearranged to find any of the three quantities. A graph of current against voltage for an ohmic conductor gives a straight line through the origin, with gradient equal to 1/resistance.

Charge flow in a circuit is measured in coulombs (C). The relationship between charge, current and time is: Q = It. One coulomb is the charge transferred when one ampere flows for one second. In metallic conductors, electric current is carried by electrons moving through the metal lattice. Conventional current flows from positive to negative, which is opposite to the direction of electron flow.

Circuits.intro: Electrical circuits can be arranged in series or parallel. Each arrangement has different rules for current, voltage and resistance.
Circuits.mnemonic: "Series Voltages Add — Parallel Currents Add" — the key rule for each circuit type in one sentence.
Circuits.diagram:
🖼️
Diagram: Series and Parallel Circuits
Image coming soon

sections.title: Series Circuits
sections.text: In a series circuit, all components share the same current and the total voltage is divided between them.
points: Single loop — all components connected in one continuous path; no branches
Same current — the same current flows through every component in the loop
Voltages add — Vtotal = V₁ + V₂ + V₃; the supply voltage is shared between components
Resistances add — Rtotal = R₁ + R₂; adding more components increases total resistance
Break in circuit — if one component fails, the whole circuit stops; all go off

sections.title: Parallel Circuits
sections.text: In a parallel circuit, each branch receives the full supply voltage and carries its own share of the total current.
points: Separate branches — components on independent paths between the same two points
Same voltage — the full supply voltage appears across every branch
Currents split — total current = sum of branch currents: Itotal = I₁ + I₂
Lower resistance — total resistance is less than the smallest individual resistance; more paths = less resistance
Independent branches — if one branch breaks, others continue to work; used in household wiring

sections.title: Circuit Symbols and Measurement
sections.text: Knowing standard circuit symbols and how to place measuring instruments correctly is essential for exam diagrams.
points: Ammeter — measures current; connected in series in the circuit; has very low resistance
Voltmeter — measures potential difference; connected in parallel across a component; has very high resistance
Thermistor — resistance decreases as temperature increases; used in temperature sensors
LDR (light-dependent resistor) — resistance decreases as light intensity increases; used in light sensors
Diode — allows current in one direction only; used to convert AC to DC

keyTerms.def: Circuit where components are connected in a single loop — same current throughout
Circuit where components are on separate branches — same voltage across each branch
Instrument measuring current — connected in series
Instrument measuring potential difference — connected in parallel
A resistor whose resistance decreases as temperature increases
Light-dependent resistor — resistance decreases as light intensity increases
In series: sum of all resistances. In parallel: less than the smallest individual resistance.

examTips: Series: same current, voltages add. Parallel: same voltage, currents add. Learn these rules — they come up every year.
Ammeter = series (low resistance). Voltmeter = parallel (high resistance) — connecting them the wrong way is a common error.
Adding more parallel branches reduces total resistance — always explain why using the concept of more current paths.
commonMistakes: Saying voltages are the same in series — voltages are shared in series and the SAME in PARALLEL.
Connecting ammeter in parallel or voltmeter in series — this is experimentally wrong and loses method marks.
Forgetting that adding resistors in parallel always reduces total resistance below the smallest individual value.
clozePassages: In a series circuit, components are connected in a single loop. The same current flows through all components. The total resistance is the sum of individual resistances. The total potential difference is shared between components. If one component breaks, the whole circuit stops working. In a parallel circuit, components are on separate branches. The potential difference across each branch is the same. The total current is the sum of branch currents.

Ammeters measure current and are always connected in series in a circuit. Voltmeters measure potential difference and are always connected in parallel across a component. Ammeters have very low resistance to avoid affecting the circuit. Voltmeters have very high resistance so they draw minimal current. These instruments allow the electrical quantities in a circuit to be measured accurately.

The total resistance of components in series is found by adding individual resistances: R = R₁ + R₂. For parallel circuits, the total resistance is lower than any individual resistance. Adding more components in parallel provides more paths for current, decreasing total resistance. Most household circuits are wired in parallel so that each appliance receives the full mains voltage and can be switched independently.

Domestic Electricity.intro: Mains electricity in the UK is alternating current (AC) at 230V and 50Hz. Understanding how it is safely used in the home is required for P2.
Domestic Electricity.mnemonic: "Brown Lives Near Earth" — Brown = Live, Neutral = blue (Near), Earth = green/yellow — the three plug wire colours.
Domestic Electricity.diagram:
🖼️
Diagram: Three-Pin Plug and Domestic Electricity
Image coming soon

sections.title: AC vs DC
sections.text: The two types of electric current have different properties and are suited to different applications.
points: AC (alternating current) — direction of current reverses periodically; UK mains supply is 230 V at 50 Hz
DC (direct current) — current flows in one direction only; produced by batteries and cells
50 Hz — UK mains alternates 50 times per second (50 complete cycles per second)
Why AC for mains? — AC can be transformed to very high voltages for efficient transmission over long distances
DC for devices — most electronic components require DC; phone chargers convert AC to DC

sections.title: The Three-Pin Plug
sections.text: The UK three-pin plug is designed for safety, with colour-coded wires and a fuse to protect against overcurrent.
points: Live (brown) — carries current at 230 V; the dangerous wire
Neutral (blue) — completes circuit at 0 V; current returns via this wire
Earth (green/yellow) — safety wire; connected to metal case; provides low-resistance path to earth if fault develops
Fuse — in the live wire; thin wire that melts if current too high, breaking the circuit
Cable grip — holds the cable in place to prevent wires being pulled loose

sections.title: Fuses and Circuit Breakers
sections.text: Safety devices protect circuits and people by automatically breaking the circuit if a dangerous overcurrent occurs.
points: Fuse — thin wire in live wire that melts if current exceeds rating; must be replaced after blowing
Circuit breaker — electronic switch that trips if current too high; can be reset by flipping the switch
Choose fuse rating — select the fuse rating just above the normal operating current of the appliance
RCD (residual current device) — detects difference in current between live and neutral; trips instantly; protects against electric shock
How earth + fuse work together — if live touches metal casing: current flows through earth wire → large current → fuse melts → circuit breaks

keyTerms.def: Current that reverses direction periodically — mains supply
Current that flows in one direction only — batteries
A safety device that melts and breaks the circuit if current is too high
Safety wire that provides a low-resistance path to earth if appliance develops a fault
Residual current device — detects a difference between live and neutral currents and trips the circuit
An automatic switch that trips and cuts the circuit if current exceeds a set value — can be reset
Number of complete AC cycles per second — measured in hertz (Hz); UK mains = 50 Hz

examTips: Live = brown, Neutral = blue, Earth = green/yellow. Learn the colours — they come up in almost every P2 exam.
Earth wire prevents shock — if live wire touches metal casing, current flows to earth through earth wire, blowing the fuse.
AC frequency in UK = 50 Hz (50 complete cycles per second) — not 50 V or 50 A.
commonMistakes: Saying neutral wire carries current at high voltage — neutral is at 0 V; it is the live wire that is at 230 V.
Forgetting the earth wire's function — it is a safety device, not needed for the circuit to operate normally.
Mixing up fuses and circuit breakers — fuses must be replaced, circuit breakers can be reset.
clozePassages: Alternating current (AC) constantly changes direction. UK mains electricity is AC at 230 V and a frequency of 50 Hz. Direct current (DC) flows in one direction only and is produced by batteries and cells. The live wire in a plug is brown and carries the alternating voltage. The neutral wire is blue and completes the circuit. The earth wire is green-yellow and is a safety wire to prevent electric shocks.

A three-pin plug connects appliances safely to the mains. The fuse is in series with the live wire and melts if the current becomes too high, breaking the circuit and preventing fire or damage. The earth wire connects the metal case of an appliance to the ground — if a fault causes the case to become live, current flows to earth and blows the fuse. Circuit breakers perform the same function but can be reset rather than replaced.

Fuses and circuit breakers are safety devices that protect circuits from excessive current. A fuse contains a thin wire that melts if the current exceeds its rated value. A circuit breaker contains a switch that trips automatically. Both break the circuit to prevent overheating and fire. The correct fuse rating should be slightly above the normal operating current of the appliance. Residual current devices (RCDs) offer additional protection against electric shock.

Power and Energy.intro: Power is the rate of energy transfer. Electrical power depends on both current and voltage.
Power and Energy.mnemonic: "PIV — Power Is Voltage times current" — P = IV — and don't forget P = I²R for when V is missing.

🖼️
Diagram: Power and Energy in Circuits
Image coming soon

sections.title: Power Formulae
sections.text: Three versions of the power equation allow you to calculate power from any two of the three electrical quantities.
points: P = IV — power equals current × voltage; works for any electrical component
P = I²R — use when voltage is not given; derived from P = IV and V = IR
P = V²/R — use when current is not given; also derived from P = IV and V = IR
Example — a kettle takes 13 A from 230 V: P = 13 × 230 = 2990 W ≈ 3 kW
Units — power in watts (W); 1 kW = 1000 W

callout.label: Formulae
callout.text: P = I × V (Power = Current × Voltage). Also: P = I² × R and P = V²/R. Power in watts (W).

sections.title: Energy Transfer and Bills
sections.text: Energy is power multiplied by time, and electricity bills are calculated using kilowatt-hours as the unit of energy.
points: E = Pt — energy equals power × time; energy in joules, power in W, time in seconds
E = QV — energy equals charge × voltage; an alternative energy formula
Kilowatt-hour (kWh) — the commercial unit of electrical energy; 1 kWh = 3,600,000 J
Cost calculation — cost = power (kW) × time (hours) × price per kWh
Example — a 2 kW heater running for 3 hours at 30p/kWh: cost = 2 × 3 × 0.30 = £1.80

callout.label: Energy Formula
callout.text: E = P × t (Energy = Power × Time). Energy in joules (J) when time in seconds. E = Q × V (Energy = Charge × Voltage).

sections.title: Power in Transmission
sections.text: Understanding P = I²R explains why the National Grid transmits electricity at high voltage and low current to minimise energy loss.
points: P = I²R — power lost in a cable depends on the square of the current
High voltage, low current — step-up transformers increase voltage; lower current reduces cable losses
Example — doubling voltage halves current; power loss in cables drops by factor of 4
Step-down transformers — reduce voltage to safe levels (230 V) at substations near homes
Why it matters — without high-voltage transmission, a large fraction of generated power would be wasted as heat

keyTerms.def: Rate of energy transfer — measured in watts (W)
Unit of power = 1 joule per second
Unit of energy used in electricity billing = 3.6 MJ
The SI unit of energy — 1 J = 1 W × 1 s
E = Pt — energy transferred equals power multiplied by time in seconds
The high-voltage network that transmits electricity from power stations to homes and businesses

examTips: P = IV is the most important power formula. Also know P = I²R for when V is not given — it appears in higher-grade questions.
For electricity bills: use kW and hours; multiply by cost per kWh — never use watts for bill calculations.
In transmission questions: explain that high voltage means low current, and lower current means less power wasted (P = I²R).
commonMistakes: Confusing power (rate of energy transfer, in watts) with energy (total amount transferred, in joules).
Using watts instead of kilowatts in electricity cost calculations — always convert W to kW before calculating bills.
Forgetting to convert time to seconds when using E = Pt in joules — if using kWh, time must be in hours.
clozePassages: Power is the rate of energy transfer, measured in watts (W). It can be calculated as P = E/t (energy divided by time) or P = IV (current × potential difference). One watt equals one joule per second. A 60 W light bulb transfers 60 J of energy every second. The kilowatt-hour (kWh) is the unit of energy used by electricity companies — it equals the energy used by a 1 kW appliance in one hour.

The energy transferred by an electrical appliance can be calculated using E = Pt (power × time) or E = IVt (current × voltage × time). The cost of electricity is calculated by multiplying the number of kilowatt-hours by the price per kWh. Choosing energy-efficient appliances with lower power ratings reduces electricity bills and carbon emissions. The energy rating label on appliances helps consumers compare efficiency.

Electrical power in a resistor can be calculated using P = I²R or P = V²/R. These equations are derived from combining P = IV with V = IR. Appliances with high resistance generate more heat when the same current flows through them. This is the principle behind electric heaters and toasters. In power transmission, using high voltage reduces current, which reduces the power lost as heat in the cables (P = I²R).

Static Electricity.intro: Static electricity is the build-up of electrical charge on insulating materials. It occurs when electrons are transferred by friction.
Static Electricity.mnemonic: "Friction Electrons Negative, Positive Loses" — Friction transfers Electrons; the gainer is Negative, the loser is Positive.
Static Electricity.diagram:
🖼️
Diagram: Static Electricity and Electric Fields
Image coming soon

sections.title: Charging by Friction
sections.text: When two insulators are rubbed together, electrons transfer from one to the other, leaving both objects charged.
points: Electron transfer — only electrons move during friction charging; protons remain fixed in nuclei
Gaining electrons — object that gains electrons becomes negatively charged
Losing electrons — object that loses electrons becomes positively charged
Like charges repel — two negative or two positive objects push each other apart
Unlike charges attract — positive and negative objects are attracted to each other

sections.title: Electric Fields
sections.text: Every charged object creates an electric field — a region of space where other charges experience a force.
points: Field lines — show the direction of force on a positive test charge; point away from + and towards −
Radial field — field lines spread outward from an isolated point charge; weaker further away
Uniform field — between two parallel plates with opposite charges; field lines are parallel and equally spaced
Force on charge — a charged object in an electric field experiences a force in the direction of field lines (if positive)
Field strength — greatest where field lines are closest together

sections.title: Uses and Hazards of Static Electricity
sections.text: Static electricity has important practical applications but also poses hazards that require engineering solutions.
points: Electrostatic spray painting — charged paint droplets attracted to earthed object; even coverage, less waste
Photocopiers — charged drum attracts toner powder; toner transferred to paper by static forces
Defibrillators — store large static charge on capacitor; discharge through patient to restart heart
Fuel tanker hazard — static builds up from fuel movement; earthing prevents sparks near flammable fuel
Lightning conductors — pointed conductor on buildings provides easy path for charge to discharge safely to earth

keyTerms.def: Electrical charge that builds up on insulating materials — does not flow
The region around a charged object where forces act on other charges
Connecting a charged object to earth to safely discharge it
Redistribution of charges in a neutral object when a charged object is brought near
Lines showing the direction and relative strength of an electric field; point from + to −
A material that allows charge to flow freely through it — metals are good conductors
A material that does not allow charge to flow — insulators can build up static charge

examTips: Only electrons move when charging by friction — protons stay in the nucleus; state this explicitly in exam answers.
Like charges repel; unlike charges attract — apply this to all static electricity questions about forces.
Electric field lines always point from positive to negative; they never cross each other.
commonMistakes: Saying protons move during friction charging — only electrons are transferred; protons are fixed in nuclei.
Confusing static electricity (charge that stays on an insulator) with current electricity (continuous flow of charge through a conductor).
Drawing electric field lines pointing from negative to positive — they always go from positive to negative.
clozePassages: Static electricity builds up when certain materials are rubbed together, causing electrons to be transferred from one material to the other. The material that gains electrons becomes negatively charged; the one that loses electrons becomes positively charged. Like charges repel each other and unlike charges attract. Static electricity can cause sparks, which is a hazard near flammable materials.

An electric field exists around any charged object. A second charged object in this field experiences a force. The field is strongest near the object and weaker further away. Field lines show the direction of the force on a positive charge. Electric fields between parallel plates are uniform. Lightning occurs when the electric field between clouds and the ground is strong enough to cause a large discharge of charge through the air.

Static electricity has many practical uses. In electrostatic spray painting, charged droplets are attracted to the earthed object being painted, giving even coverage and reducing waste. Photocopiers use electrostatic attraction to transfer toner powder to paper. Defibrillators deliver a controlled electric shock to restart a stopped heart. Earthing provides a safe path for charge to flow to the ground, preventing dangerous build-up of static charge.
